context.in_practice: Route 1: watch handles a broken config the same way every other command does. It stops right away with exit code 4 and never prints its usual startup line. That line is treated as a promise that watching has really begun, so it only appears once the config has loaded. Scripts and people can rely on it: if the line shows up, watching is live; exit code 4 means the config was the problem. Route 2: this case was never considered. Nobody decided what happens when watch starts with a config it can't load, so the behavior is whatever the code happens to do. It might print the startup line and then fail, keep running with nothing loaded, or exit with a code that differs from the other commands. Nothing was run for either route, so neither behavior has been checked.
context.stakes: If someone starts watch mode while the config file is broken or unreadable, they need to know right away that nothing is being watched. Otherwise they may believe changes are being tracked when they are not.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 needs watch to load the config before announcing itself, in line with the other commands. Route 2 costs nothing now, but it leaves this failure's behavior undefined and possibly inconsistent or misleading.

plan_why: The question is only about how `troupe config watch` behaves when it starts with an unloadable config, and the sandbox forbids running `watch`. Implementations that never handled this case may print `watching <dir>` and then keep running until they are interrupted, so the 20-second limit would cut them off. Other commands already exit 4 on an unloadable config under every route, so they don't show the difference.
